n: The guide moves from the porch into the temple building itself. The entrance pillars are six cubits thick—massive, as befits the house of God.

f.g: Here simply “tent” or dwelling—an echo of the wilderness tabernacle where God dwelt among Israel.

n: The main hall, the Holy Place, is forty by twenty cubits—exactly the size of the Holy Place in Solomon’s temple.

f.w: forty cubits: and the breadth, twenty cubits

n: Only the guide goes further inward; Ezekiel, though a priest, stays back. The entrances narrow as one approaches the holiest room—a picture of increasing sacredness.

f.g: Ezekiel does not enter the most holy place himself.

n: The Most Holy Place is a perfect cube in floor plan, twenty by twenty cubits, as in Solomon’s temple. Here God’s presence dwelt; in ancient Israel only the high priest entered, once a year.

f.w: This is the most holy place

n: The temple’s walls are six cubits thick, and along the outside are side rooms four cubits wide—likely storerooms for temple supplies.

f.g: Storage rooms built against the outer walls.

n: The side rooms rise three stories, thirty to a level. Their beams rest on ledges rather than being cut into the temple wall, so the sanctuary wall is not pierced.

f.w: they had not hold in the wall of the house

n: The side rooms get wider on each higher floor because the temple wall steps inward. A stairway or ramp leads up through the levels.

f.g: A stairway or ramp leading upward.

n: The temple stands on a raised platform six long cubits high—lifting the sanctuary above its surroundings.

f.w: a full reed of six great cubits

n: The outer wall of the side rooms is five cubits thick, with an open terrace beyond it.
A twenty-cubit open space surrounds the temple, separating it from the priests’ buildings.
Doors from the side rooms open north and south onto the terrace, which is five cubits wide.

f.g: An open, unbuilt area or terrace.

n: Behind the temple on the west stands a large separate building, seventy by ninety cubits. Its purpose isn’t stated; it may have been for storage or service.

f.g: A restricted or set-apart yard behind the temple.

n: The temple and its surroundings measure a hundred cubits long—another perfect, round number showing completeness.
The east front of the temple with its adjoining yard is also a hundred cubits wide, so the temple area is a perfect square.
The western building and its galleries are a hundred cubits as well. Everything fits a symmetrical, harmonious plan.

f.g: Possibly terraces or colonnades; the Hebrew word is uncertain.

n: The interior is paneled with wood from floor to windows, with framed windows and three levels of galleries.
The walls inside and out, even above the doors, are all decorated according to careful measure.
Carvings alternate cherubim and palm trees. In Solomon’s temple the same designs recalled Eden, where cherubim guarded the way to the tree of life.

f.g: Unlike the four-faced cherubim of Ezekiel 1, these show two faces in the flat carving.

n: Each cherub has the face of a man turned toward one palm and the face of a lion toward another, repeated all around the house.
The cherubim and palms cover the walls from floor to above the doors.
The doorposts are square, and the entrance to the sanctuary matches the outer one—consistency throughout.
A wooden altar stands before the Most Holy Place. The guide calls it “the table that is before the LORD,” likely corresponding to the table of shewbread or the incense altar.

f.w: This is the table that is before the LORD

n: Both the Holy Place and the Most Holy Place have doors.
Each door has two folding leaves that turn on hinges, like Solomon’s temple doors.
The doors bear the same cherubim and palm carvings as the walls. A wooden canopy or threshold covers the outside of the porch.

f.g: Possibly a wooden canopy or overhang; the Hebrew is uncertain.

n: The porch walls and side rooms have narrow windows and palm decorations. The whole building is beautiful and orderly—fitting for the place God would dwell.
